title: Xiaomi's Three Chips: Trading Resources for Time, Betting on an On-Device AI Paradigm Shift
dek: Xiaomi releases three Xuanjie chips in one go, aggressively betting on memory interconnect, 3D stacking, and an all-AI architecture. It trades resources for time, betting on an on-device AI paradigm shift and vertical integration, but still lags top-tier chip companies.
why: This episode offers an in-depth analysis of the technical choices and strategic logic behind Xiaomi's three chips. It is information-dense, with clear analogies for key technologies like memory interconnect and 3D stacking. Worth a listen for chip industry professionals and investors following Xiaomi.
who: Investors focused on Xiaomi's chip efforts, chip industry engineers, product managers, and tech professionals wanting to understand on-device AI trends.
skip: The first 3 minutes discussing the definition of self-development can be skipped; go straight to the technical analysis.

points.h: Chip capability is about system definition, not IP self-reliance
points.body: To judge whether a company can make chips, don't just count how many IP blocks it handcrafts; look at how much system definition power it holds. Xiaomi's Xuanjie O1 uses ARM IP for CPU and GPU, but system integration and physical implementation are its own. Apple and Qualcomm are strong because they iterate yearly and tape out continuously—something latecomers lack. Xiaomi doesn't have a decade to learn slowly, so it chooses an aggressive path, advancing multiple high-risk technology lines simultaneously.

points.h: O1's poor energy efficiency stems from a missing shared water tank
points.body: The Xuanjie O1 lacks a system-level cache (SLC), causing power consumption to spike under heavy GPU load and hurting energy efficiency. An SLC is like a shared water tank in a residential complex: the closer data is to compute units, the faster access and lower power. The O1 has many GPU cores but limited DDR bandwidth, so many cores wait for data, keeping utilization low—this is the bandwidth wall. The O3 adds a 16MB SLC, splits it into multiple cache blocks distributed across the chip, and designs an on-chip network scheduling system to handle data consistency and access conflicts.

points.h: ARM's generic bus forces Xuanjie to build its own
points.body: ARM's off-the-shelf CHI+CMN solution is too generic, retaining compatibility and redundancy that hinder customization for Xuanjie. The O3 instead develops its own X-Ring unified fabric, compatible with CHI but defining its own interconnect protocol, along with a custom high-speed network hub and memory controller. This reduces protocol conversion overhead and lets data decide cache placement and paths based on needs. Xiaomi claims protocol conversion overhead drops 75%, and static access latency is 82 nanoseconds, 32% lower than the O1 and even lower than Apple's A19 Pro.

points.h: Compute bottleneck shifts from matrix multiplication to vector operations
points.body: The O3 adds AI units to every subsystem—CPU, GPU, ISP—so computation happens where data resides, reducing data movement. NPU core count drops from 6 to 4, but tensor compute rises to 200 TOPS because Xiaomi judges that large-model bottlenecks are expanding from matrix multiplication to vector operations like Softmax, quantization, and KV cache. Vector units are about the same area as tensor units, with 6.8 times the multiply-accumulate units of the O1, and introduce an SMT-like architecture, similar to CUDA, to handle irregular parallel tasks.

points.h: Chips and models should be co-defined by the same company
points.body: Xiaomi partners with MEMO to compress INT4 weights to 5 bits using a 5-value quantization method, with almost no accuracy loss, reducing memory bandwidth and capacity needs by 30%. The 3-billion-parameter MEMO model runs on the O3, with prefill performance up 40% and decode up 45%. This ability to co-define chips and models is the closed-loop advantage of vertical integration—no need to wait for others to define models and then adapt.

points.h: 3nm performance is squeezed out cell by cell
points.body: The O3 uses the more mature N3P process, delivering 5% better performance at same power and 5%-10% lower power at same frequency. Xiaomi also does extensive process optimization: self-developed standard cells grow from 480 in the O1 to over 2,400, covering various chip units; power delivery buffers are compressed so power and signals route from module centers, boosting transistor density by 5%. The CPU shifts from 4 clusters to 3 clusters of 10 big cores, with single-core performance up 31% and multi-core up 60%, surpassing the A19 Pro.

points.h: Near-memory computing pushes phone memory bandwidth to 1.22TB/s
points.body: The Xuanjie O100 uses wafer-level 3D stacking: one compute wafer plus two memory wafers stacked vertically, connected via hybrid bonding, forming a near-memory computing architecture. It uses thousands of shorter, denser vertical connections for high bandwidth, with lower energy per bit shift—similar to HBM for phones. Data: 28,762 data connections, bandwidth 1.22TB/s, far exceeding the tens of bits of traditional SoC-LPDDR connections. The compute layer has 14 independent cores, each paired with a RISC-V processor for control.

points.h: CXMT's value lies in co-definition, not speed grades
points.body: Xiaomi partners with CXMT to debut LPDDR6, reducing reliance on Samsung and SK Hynix. Even if CXMT offers the entry-level 10.667Gbps speed, Xiaomi can compensate for peak rate gaps with wider channels, larger SLC, and a custom memory controller. More importantly, the two co-validate and tune from the design stage, jointly defining a Chinese mobile memory subsystem solution. For CXMT, this proves its high-speed I/O and PHY capabilities, earning a seat at the next-generation mobile memory table.

points.h: Xiaomi bets not on chips but on a time window
points.body: First, it bets on an on-device computing paradigm shift: AI's weight in SoCs grows, phones become AI interaction gateways, and Xiaomi wants to be in the definer's seat. Second, it bets that vertical integration becomes a core competency for device companies: generic chips can't meet the fragmented needs of human, car, and home scenarios, so Xiaomi must own its compute architecture. Third, it bets on an uncertain time window, trading resources for time to compress the catch-up cycle, preferring to bear engineering risk rather than wait for the window to close.

points.h: Xuanjie closes faster, but still misses all three thresholds
points.body: Top-tier SoC companies need three capabilities: custom CPU/GPU microarchitecture, custom 5G baseband, and continuous multi-generation tape-outs with tens of millions of shipments. Xuanjie currently meets none, still clearly behind the first tier—it just closes faster. What truly reshapes the industry isn't a single stunning chip but the sustained iteration capability built by a group of companies. Xuanjie's larger significance is proving Xiaomi's chip efforts haven't stopped and that it's moving forward with Chinese chip industry partners.

terms.def: A cache shared by multiple compute units on a chip, like a shared water tank in a residential complex.
A wafer-level 3D stacking interconnect technology using direct copper-to-copper connections, offering high bandwidth and low power.
Placing memory and compute units close together to reduce data movement distance, improving bandwidth and energy efficiency.
A performance bottleneck where data movement capability limits performance, so adding more compute cores doesn't help.
A parallel processing architecture that can manage multiple task groups simultaneously, improving compute unit utilization.
